display_name: Tyrrell's Vat 1 Semillon, New South Wales
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "Hunter Valley's sandy alluvial loam forces Semillon into early harvest at 10.5–11.5% potential alcohol, and Tyrrell's Vat 1 goes to bottle within eight weeks. The result is a wine that starts life looking like bottled water and ends up tasting like toasted brioche fifteen years later.",
  "wine_summary": "Tyrrell’s family has worked the same Pokolbin blocks since 1858; their Vat 1 Semillon is Australia’s longest-running single-vineyard white label, first bottled in 1963. The Hunter’s cloud-covered February keeps maximum temperatures below 28°C while the vines sit on free-draining alluvial sand; the berries stay physiologically ripe without accumulating sugar, so acid remains high and alcohol stays low. That acid is the scaffolding on which the wine’s post-bottle transformation hangs: lemon shifts to toast, beeswax and roasted hazelnut while the pH never budges below 3.0, keeping the palate laser-bright for decades.",
  "terroir_expression": "The vineyard sits on the Lower Hunter’s sandy alluvial loam—essentially an old riverbed of quartz and feldspar over Permian volcanic basement. The soil holds almost no water, forcing roots to dive 3–4m for moisture stored in the underlying red duplex clays; the stress limits berry size to 0.8g and thickens skins, concentrating citrus phenolics that later read as toast. Add the maritime cloud layer that rolls in most afternoons, dropping average solar radiation by 15% compared to Barossa, and you get phenolic ripeness at 19°Brix instead of the 24–26° seen elsewhere; that’s why Hunter Semillon can be both ripe and 10.5% alcohol.",
  "vinification_summary": "Hand-picked at 19.5–20.5°Brix, whole-bunch pressed to 0.2 bar pressure, cold-settled 48h, then racked to stainless for a 14-day 16°C ferment with neutral Bordeaux yeast (to prevent vegetal thiols). Immediate sulfur addition (40ppm total) locks in the shy acidity; bottled six weeks post-ferment without fining to preserve CO₂ near 1g/L, giving the youthful wine its trademark slight spritz.",
  "food_pairing": [
    "Nashville hot chicken — the 3.0 pH cuts cayenne oil while low alcohol keeps capsaicin from flaring.",
    "Sydney rock oysters with finger-lime — the wine’s early lemon pith mirrors oyster brine and the bubbles lift shellfish sweetness.",
    "Aged Comté 24mo — as the wine develops toast and hazelnut it creates a shared Maillard echo with the cheese.",
    "Steamed barramundi with ginger-soy dressing — high acid tackles soy salt, subtle spritz refreshes between bites.",
    "Fine dining: lobster cognac bisque poured tableside; the wine’s evolved beeswax and toast play the bisque’s reduction while acidity keeps the dish from feeling heavy."
  ],
  "comparable_wines": [
    "Château Carbonnieux Blanc, Pessac-Léognan — similarly relies on low alcohol and high acid to age from citrus into toast, though sees oak.",
    "Mount Horrocks Semillon, Clare, Clare Valley — same gravity-defying aging curve but grown on terra rossa over limestone, giving slightly more lime zest.",
    "Château de Tracy Pouilly-Fumé — also starts grassy-lemon and blossoms into honeycomb, sharing Loire flint smoke absent in Hunter."
  ],
  "style_profile": "Light-bodied dry white with rapier acidity and transformative toast-and-honey development.",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drink the 2016–18 now for lime-skin tension or hold to 2035+ for full toast-hazelnut complexity; 12°C constant temperature and 65% humidity keep the natural cork supple.",
  "value_assessment": "Around $60 retail in the US, it sits between $55 Pewton Hill Semillon and $70 brokenwood Graveyard. No other ageworthy white at this price offers two decades of evolution, so the math is simple: buy.",
  "market_position": "Sommeliers in Sydney and London list it by the glass to show guests what Hunter Semillon can do; collectors buy half-cases for verticals, while casual Australian drinkers pick up a bottle because it’s still cheaper than most Chardonnays that won’t live nearly as long.",
  "insider_take": "People expect immediate pleasure from a $60 white; Vat 1 demands at least eight years to stop tasting like lemon water. If your cellar discipline is shaky, spend the money on mature releases or stick to Sauvignon Blanc—this wine punishes early opening harder than any other Australian white.",

  "drinking_window_min_years": 8,

  }

parsed.wine_summary: Tyrrell’s family has worked the same Pokolbin blocks since 1858; their Vat 1 Semillon is Australia’s longest-running single-vineyard white label, first bottled in 1963. The Hunter’s cloud-covered February keeps maximum temperatures below 28°C while the vines sit on free-draining alluvial sand; the berries stay physiologically ripe without accumulating sugar, so acid remains high and alcohol stays low. That acid is the scaffolding on which the wine’s post-bottle transformation hangs: lemon shifts to toast, beeswax and roasted hazelnut while the pH never budges below 3.0, keeping the palate laser-bright for decades.
parsed.terroir_expression: The vineyard sits on the Lower Hunter’s sandy alluvial loam—essentially an old riverbed of quartz and feldspar over Permian volcanic basement. The soil holds almost no water, forcing roots to dive 3–4m for moisture stored in the underlying red duplex clays; the stress limits berry size to 0.8g and thickens skins, concentrating citrus phenolics that later read as toast. Add the maritime cloud layer that rolls in most afternoons, dropping average solar radiation by 15% compared to Barossa, and you get phenolic ripeness at 19°Brix instead of the 24–26° seen elsewhere; that’s why Hunter Semillon can be both ripe and 10.5% alcohol.
parsed.vinification_summary: Hand-picked at 19.5–20.5°Brix, whole-bunch pressed to 0.2 bar pressure, cold-settled 48h, then racked to stainless for a 14-day 16°C ferment with neutral Bordeaux yeast (to prevent vegetal thiols). Immediate sulfur addition (40ppm total) locks in the shy acidity; bottled six weeks post-ferment without fining to preserve CO₂ near 1g/L, giving the youthful wine its trademark slight spritz.
